name: Superficial Fibromatosis

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for Superficial Fibromatosis

criteria.description: Presence of firm, palpable nodules or cords in the palmar fascia
Fixed flexion contracture of one or more fingers, typically the ring and little fingers
Histological confirmation showing fibroblast proliferation and collagen deposition without malignancy
Presence of nodules or fibrous thickening in the plantar fascia (Ledderhose disease)
Positive family history of superficial fibromatosis

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of palmar nodules or cords with fixed finger contracture plus histopathological confirmation
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is primarily clinical supported by histopathology; imaging may assist in atypical cases.

pathognomonic.notes: Firm, subcutaneous nodules localized to palmar fascia
Fixed flexion deformities primarily affecting ring and little fingers
Taut fibrous bands palpable under the skin of the palm

common.notes: Nodules on the plantar fascia (Ledderhose disease)
searchTerms: hard nodules on sole of foot

common.notes: Skin dimpling or puckering over fibrous nodules
Reduced range of motion due to contracture
Less common involvement of dorsal hand fascia

occasional.symptomName: Pain or tenderness at nodule sites

occasional.notes: Presence of knuckle pads or Garrod’s pads
Diffuse thickening noted on imaging or palpation

rare.notes: Rare nerve entrapment symptoms due to fibrous tissue
searchTerms: weakness or pain in hands and feet
nerve damage symptoms in arms or legs

imaging: Ultrasound showing hypoechoic fibrous nodules in palmar fascia
MRI demonstrating fibrous cord thickening and fascial involvement
genetic: Association with HLA class II alleles in some familial cases
No single causative gene identified; polygenic inheritance suspected
other: Histopathology showing fibroblast proliferation, dense collagen bundles, and absence of malignancy

distinguishingFeatures: Often considered synonymous but may represent a spectrum; isolated contracture without nodules suggests other causes
Absence of plantar or penile involvement
Keloids present as raised, erythematous scars following skin injury
Histology shows excessive collagen but lacks nodular fibromatosis pattern
Malignant features on histology including atypia and mitotic figures
Rapid growth and pain more common

redFlags: Severe pain disproportionate to lesion size
Neurological deficits such as numbness or weakness in affected limb
references: Luck JV Jr. Dupuytren's contracture: clinical evaluation and treatment. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 1980
Hindocha S, et al. The pathogenesis of Dupuytren's disease. J Hand Surg Eur Vol. 2006
